definition: the head; the thing that holds your brain
example: Mi mamá dice que tengo un cabezón.
exampleTranslation: My mom says I have a big head.

hint1.text: French people loved to do this during their 1789 revolution.

hint2.text: To cut off the head of a person or animal

items.text: Cabeza and decapitate both from the latin word caput, which has also branched into English words like capital and captain. Another word that possibly came from caput is chef, as in a professional cook. According to the Oxford English Dictionary, it may have come from the French term “chef de cuisine,” which meant a head or executive chef.

items.text: Renaissance and nacer both come from the latin root nascĕre, which is also the root of English words like native and nation. If you go further back to the Proto-Indo-European (a language from which many modern languages evolved from) root genə-, then you can find that related words also include indigenous and gene.

sources: Oxford English Dictionary. "Renaissance, n." Oxford University Press. Accessed January 8, 2026. https://www.oed.com/dictionary/renaissance_n.

definition: To grow; become bigger in size
example: Mi sobrino ha crecido mucho desde la última vez que lo vi.
exampleTranslation: My nephew has grown a lot since the last time I saw him

hint2.text: the point at which a sound or piece of music reaches its highest intensity

items.text: Crecer and crescendo both come from the latin root crescĕre, which also gave us the English words increase and crescent. According to the Merriam Webster Dictionary, the name of the crescent moon used to only refer to the phases of the moon when it was growing. The Latin root also gives us the word croissant through French, so now, when you think of the moon, you can think of both croissants and cheese.

sources: Real Academia Española. "Crecer." Diccionario de la lengua española, 23rd ed. Accessed January 1, 2026. https://dle.rae.es/crecer.

definition: warlike; describes anything to do with war
example: Los periodistas suelen cubrir noticias en zonas belicas.
exampleTranslation: Journalists usually cover news in warzones.

hint1.text: The first half of the movie "Gone With the Wind" takes place in this time period

hint2.text: A term used to describe a period of time before war, usually referring to the American Civil War

items.text: Antebellum and Bélico both come from the latin root bellĭcus, which also gave us the word belligerent. The prefix ante- in antebellum literally means “before”(an easy catch if you know Spanish!).

sources: Real Academia Española. "Bélico." Diccionario de la lengua española, 23rd ed. Accessed January 2, 2026. https://dle.rae.es/b%C3%A9lico.
